channel.title: Cutefish
channel.description: A Linux distribution for people at home on a Mac. Its desktop, compositor and built-in apps are written from scratch in C++ and Skia.

item.title: What's new in Cutefish: 17 languages, Preview and software updates
item.description: Cutefish now speaks 17 languages, opens images and PDFs in its new Preview app, installs its own updates and comes with its own installer.
item.content:encoded:
The first Cutefish ISO went up on October 20. A lot has changed since then. Here are the biggest changes.

17 languages

Cutefish now speaks 17 languages: English, Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese, French, German, Russian, Japanese, Korean, Italian, Polish, Czech, Indonesian, Vietnamese, Malay, and Chinese in three forms: Simplified, Traditional for Taiwan, and Traditional for Hong Kong.

Every part of the desktop is translated: the Dock, the menu bar, the launcher, Settings, and every app that comes with Cutefish. If you change the language in Settings, open apps switch right away. You don’t have to log out. Dates, times and numbers follow your region, which you choose on the same Language & Region page.

You can pick the language on the installer’s first screen, and the installed system starts in it.

If a translation reads wrong in your language, you can fix it with a pull request to that app’s repository on GitHub.

Preview

Preview is a new app for images and PDF documents. It opens PDFs with page thumbnails and the table of contents in the sidebar. You can search a document, select and copy its text, and follow its links. Images can be zoomed, panned and rotated. Rotating a JPEG keeps its quality, because the picture itself is not encoded again.

Preview is now the default app for images and PDFs.

Software updates

Cutefish checks for updates once a day. Settings has a new Software Update page that lists what is waiting. You can install updates there and keep working while they install, or let Cutefish install them the next time you restart.

Our own installer

The ISO now comes with Cutefish’s own installer. It walks you through the language, the disk, your account and the time zone, and includes manual partitioning. There is also an ISO for arm64 computers now, next to the one for amd64.

Dock magnification

Dock icons can now grow as the pointer passes over them, and the icons around them grow a little less. Turn it on with the Magnification slider in Settings > Dock & Desktop.

The desktop

  • Launcher folders. Drag one app onto another in the launcher to group them into a folder.
  • Dock. An app’s icon hops while it starts.
  • Glass. Menus and the menu bar’s panels, such as Control Center, share a new glass look. The Dock has a glass of its own, and Settings > Dock & Desktop > Glass effect sets how tinted it is. Settings > Appearance > Reduce Transparency turns the glass off.
  • App menus in the menu bar. Files, Terminal, Text Editor and the other apps now show their menus at the top of the screen.
  • Calculator. A new keypad with round keys.
  • Startup. A new boot menu theme and a new splash screen with the Cutefish logo.

Try it

Nightly ISOs and the APT repository for Debian 13 are at download.cutefish.org. If you already run Cutefish, an update brings all of this to you.

item.title: Mac apps on Cutefish: the first milestone
item.description: Reef has reached its first milestone. Real Mac apps install from their disk images and run completely, from a text editor and a terminal to a feed reader with a real web engine.
item.content:encoded:
Ten days ago we wrote about Reef, the part of Cutefish that runs apps made for the Mac. Today it reaches its first milestone. Real Mac apps install from the same disk images a Mac user downloads, and run completely on Cutefish: a text editor, a terminal, a feed reader, an archive utility and a speed test. Here is what that took, and what changed along the way.

More apps run

NetNewsWire, the feed reader, runs completely: the sidebar, the article list, the article view, the toolbar, swipe actions, adding and refreshing feeds, all three settings panes, and the unread count on its Dock icon. Its articles are drawn by a real web engine, which Reef didn’t have ten days ago.

Ghostty, the terminal, runs with its Metal renderer, its inspector and custom shaders. It got a post of its own: The Mac version of Ghostty, on Linux.

Open a Mac app from the Dock and its icon hops once while the app starts, the same as every other app on Cutefish. Here it is with Ghostty, first at normal speed, then up close and slowed down four times.

Keka, the archive utility, compresses and extracts zip and tar.gz archives.

Speedtest by Ookla runs a full test (latency, download, upload, packet loss) and keeps a history of past results. In the screenshot we blurred our results, the test server and our provider.

CotEditor, which mostly worked last time, now remembers its windows. Quit it with untitled documents still open, and they come back, text and all, the next time you open it. Its windows can also be grouped into tabs and go full screen, with the menu bar sliding in when you move the pointer to the top of the screen.

Installing an app

Mac apps usually come as a disk image, a .dmg file. On Cutefish you install them the same way you would on a Mac. Double-click the disk image in Files and it opens under Locations. Then drag the app into your Applications folder. Files reads these images itself.

An installed app shows up in the launcher and can be pinned to the Dock. To remove it, drag it to the Trash. Nothing else is written anywhere: the folder is the app.

If an app needs something Reef can’t do yet, a dialog tells you so, instead of the app silently failing to open.

Opening your files

A Mac app tells the system which kinds of documents it can open. Cutefish reads that list, so once an app is installed, Files offers it for those documents, right next to the Linux apps. Right-click a Swift source file and choose Open with, and CotEditor is there:

Choose it, and CotEditor opens the file with its syntax colouring, like any other editor would. If CotEditor is already running, the file opens in a new window of the same app.

It works the same way for archives. Keka offers itself for a zip file:

Keka extracts it, posts a Cutefish notification when it’s done, and shows the extracted folder in a Files window, the same steps it takes on a Mac.

What’s new underneath

Each new app needs parts of macOS that no earlier app used. These were the biggest:

  • A web engine. Many Mac apps show part of their interface as a web page, through a web view. We ported WebKit, the open-source web engine, to Cutefish. The engine itself is WebKit’s own, and the layer that connects it to our display and input is ours. NetNewsWire is the first app to use it.
  • Core Data, the database layer many Mac apps store their data in. It writes the same file format as on a Mac, with migrations between data model versions.
  • Metal, the Mac’s graphics interface. Reef runs it on OpenGL and translates an app’s Metal shaders when they load.
  • Network framework, which newer apps use to open connections and follow network changes.
  • Window restoration and autosave, so apps come back the way you left them.
  • Scrolling that follows the Mac’s wheel acceleration and touchpad momentum, so scrolling in a Mac app feels the way its developers expected.

All of this brings Reef to about 460,000 lines of our own code across more than 80 frameworks. It was 300,000 lines ten days ago.

Faster and lighter

We keep measuring Mac apps against Cutefish’s own apps on the same laptop. Some of the changes since the first post:

  • A CotEditor frame while scrolling takes about 3 ms to draw, down from 4.4 ms. Cutefish Text Editor takes 1.2 ms.
  • CotEditor stays responsive in a file of 100,000 lines. Before, typing in it froze the window. Now a key press reaches the screen in about 70 ms.
  • CotEditor needs 146 MB of memory with a 20,000-line file open, down from 245 MB.
  • Ghostty draws a frame of live window resizing in 2.4 ms instead of 6.7 ms. Closing one of its tabs now frees the tab’s memory and ends its shell.
  • NetNewsWire, Ghostty and CotEditor open 10 to 40 ms sooner.

There’s still a gap to native apps, and we’re working on it.

What’s next

Reef will ship in Cutefish as soon as possible, so you can try these apps yourself.

item.title: The Mac version of Ghostty, on Linux
item.description: Ghostty comes in a Mac version and a Linux version. On Cutefish you can run either. We put them side by side and explain why we reach for the Mac one.
item.content:encoded:
Ghostty is a popular terminal app, the window where you type commands. It comes in two versions, one for the Mac and one for Linux. On most Linux systems you can only use the Linux version. On Cutefish you can also run the Mac version, thanks to Reef, the part of Cutefish that runs Mac apps.

We tried both, with the same settings and Ghostty’s standard look, and the Mac version gives the better experience. Here they are next to each other, the Mac version on the left.

It looks at home

The Mac version’s title bar takes on the colour of the terminal, with the same three window buttons as every other Cutefish window.

The Mac version also puts all its menus in the Cutefish menu bar at the top of the screen, with the keyboard shortcut for each command written next to it. Everything Ghostty can do is a click away, and you can learn the shortcuts as you go.

Tabs sit neatly under the title, each with its shortcut, and you can split a window into several terminals.

If you like a see-through window, the Mac version softly blurs what’s behind it, title bar included, so the text stays easy to read.

It feels smooth

It opens straight into a terminal. The Mac version’s window shows the terminal from the very first moment it appears, and is ready for typing almost at once.

Scrolling glides. Flick the touchpad and the text keeps gliding and gently slows down, like everywhere else on Cutefish.

It’s the Ghostty Mac users know

The Mac version uses the same settings file and the same shortcuts as Ghostty on a Mac. If you’ve used it there, you already know it here. Mac extras come along too: the Quick Terminal drops down from the top of the screen whenever you need it, and if you close a tab by mistake, Undo brings it back within a few seconds.

How fast is it?

We timed both versions on the same laptop.

Mac version Linux version
Time until the window appears 0.18 s 0.39 s
Time until you can type 0.21 s 0.44 s
Time from a key press to the letter on screen 16 ms 18 ms
Time to show a 50 MB file 2.4 s 2.5 s
Stutters while typing, scrolling and resizing none none
Memory used 147 MB 132 MB

The Mac version opens in less than half the time. Once it’s open, both are equally quick: letters appear just as fast, long output scrolls by just as fast, and neither stutters.

The trade-offs

The Mac version uses about 15 MB more memory, because it brings along the parts of Cutefish that run Mac apps. It also works the processor harder while you resize the window or scroll, which on a laptop means a little more battery. For everyday typing you won’t feel a difference.

Our recommendation

If you use Ghostty on Cutefish, we recommend the Mac version. It opens faster, fits in with the rest of the desktop, and feels smoother to use.

item.title: Running Mac apps on Cutefish
item.description: Cutefish will be able to run apps made for the Mac, menu bar apps included. What that takes, how it differs from Darling and Wine, and what runs so far.
item.content:encoded:
Cutefish will be able to run apps made for the Mac. Not just regular apps with windows, but also the small menu bar apps that sit next to the clock. A Mac app on Cutefish opens in a normal window, puts its menus in our menu bar and shows up in the Dock, like any other app on the desktop.

Every app in this screenshot is a Mac app. We did not modify or recompile any of them for Linux. They are the same downloads a Mac user would get.

Why this is hard

A Mac app does very little on its own. To open a window, show a menu, draw a line of text or work out what day it is, it calls into macOS: AppKit for windows and controls, Foundation for text, dates and files, Core Graphics for drawing, SwiftUI for newer interfaces, and dozens of other frameworks.

None of that exists on Linux. To run a Mac app we have to provide all of it ourselves, and it has to behave the way macOS does. When our answer is even slightly off, the app lays out its window wrong, draws nothing, or crashes.

In practice that means writing our own version of a large part of macOS’s programming interfaces. We call it Reef. It is over 300,000 lines of code across more than 70 frameworks, and AppKit and Foundation alone are over 70,000 lines each. Underneath sit a loader for Mac programs (they use a different binary format, Mach-O), an Objective-C runtime, support for Swift and a low-level system library. Even so, this covers only part of macOS, which has tens of thousands of these functions.

How we work

Nobody knows exactly which parts of macOS a given app needs, so we can’t write everything up front. We go app by app. We run a real Mac app and look at where it breaks: a missing function, a window drawn wrong, a button that does nothing. Then we work out what a Mac does there, implement it as a general feature rather than a fix for that one app, add a test, and run the app again.

Each app makes the next one easier, since apps share most of what they use. But how much is left is genuinely unknown. The next app can always reach for something nobody has used yet.

Some of what we run into:

  • A drop-down and the label beside it should share a text baseline. We measured the baseline from a slightly different edge than macOS does, and the drop-downs in settings windows sat a few points off their labels.
  • macOS tints an image automatically when its name ends in “Template”. We didn’t, and one app’s window buttons came out as thick black rings.
  • Asking for a redraw while a window is being prepared for drawing shouldn’t trigger another one. In our code it did, and an idle window was redrawing more than a hundred times a second.
  • Apps check which version of macOS they’re on and change their behaviour, so every version difference is a decision for us.
  • Newer apps use SwiftUI, whose internals Apple doesn’t publish. We build it from the documentation and compare our output with a real Mac, pixel by pixel.

Part of the desktop

Mac apps use the same building blocks as every other Cutefish app. Our graphics toolkit draws their windows, text and controls. Our compositor gives them the same shadows, outlines and animations as other windows, and their menus get the same glass. Our shell puts their menus in the Cutefish menu bar, their icons in the Dock and their entries in the launcher.

Menu bar apps were the real test. On a Mac, Itsycal draws a small icon with the date in the menu bar and drops a calendar from it when you click. Cutefish has status item support designed for exactly this: the app draws its own item at whatever width it needs, and its popup opens right underneath it.

What runs

Itsycal works completely: the date in the status bar, the calendar popup, the right-click menu and the settings window.

TextMate, the text editor, and Hex Fiend, the hex editor, open and edit files. Below, Hex Fiend is looking at a Linux program. CotEditor, a newer editor built partly with SwiftUI, opens, edits and saves files, with its syntax colouring, inspector, find panel and settings working.

Things 3, the to-do app, runs, and parts of it are drawn by our own SwiftUI. It isn’t finished yet.

How fast it is

Reef doesn’t emulate a processor or translate instructions. A Mac app’s own code runs directly on your CPU, the same way a Linux program does. What costs time is the part we wrote: our AppKit, Foundation and SwiftUI have to do the work macOS does for the app, and they are much younger than Apple’s.

To see where we stand, we compared CotEditor, a Mac text editor built with AppKit and SwiftUI, with Cutefish’s own text editor on the same laptop. Both open the same files and get the same input.

CotEditor on Reef Cutefish Text Editor
Start to first frame 235 ms 115 ms
Open a 4,000-line file 0.36 s 0.12 s
Open a 20,000-line file 0.50 s 0.12 s
Key press to the letter on screen 21 ms 18 ms
CPU time to type 80 characters 1.4 s 0.17 s
Time to draw a frame while scrolling 4.4 ms 1.2 ms
Time to draw a frame while resizing the window 3.8 ms 1.2 ms
Scrolling and live window resizing 60 fps 60 fps

What you feel is close: text appears within a few milliseconds of the native editor, files open in well under a second, and scrolling and resizing keep up with the screen. What you don’t see is the work behind it. CotEditor still uses several times the CPU to get there, which costs battery.

When this post first went up, typing 80 characters took 1.9 s of CPU time, a scrolling frame took 6.0 ms and a frame of live resizing 7.3 ms, with two frames drawn for every step of the resize. Since then:

  • Scrolling moves the pixels already on screen and draws only the strip that comes into view, instead of redrawing all the visible text.
  • Our SwiftUI keeps the parts of a view that didn’t change, and keeps their measured sizes, instead of rebuilding and measuring the whole tree.
  • Typing redraws only the lines a change touches, and work handed between background threads wakes far fewer of them.
  • Resizing draws one frame per step, and no longer measures every menu item of every toolbar pop-up on each frame. It uses less than half the CPU it did.

The rest of the gap is mostly the app’s own work: CotEditor lays out three nested split views and wraps its text again for every new window width, and it asks for some of its redraws itself. These were problems in our code, not limits of the approach, and we’re still working on them.

What won’t work

Anything that goes through Apple’s servers is out of reach. That includes the App Store. A Mac app on Cutefish can’t sell you a subscription or an in-app purchase, and one you bought on a Mac won’t carry over. Apps sold only in the Mac App Store can’t be installed at all, because the download is tied to an Apple account. We need a version from the developer’s own website.

iCloud is the same. Sign in with Apple doesn’t work, and an app that syncs through iCloud keeps its data on your computer.

If an app sells licences on its own website or syncs through its own service, none of this applies.

Where the code comes from

Reef is our own code. It doesn’t use code from Darling or from Wine. We don’t take apart or copy Apple’s closed macOS software, and we don’t use Apple’s developer kit. When we need to know how something should behave, we read Apple’s documentation, look at what the app is asking for, and compare with the same app running on a Mac.

We do build on the parts of its platform that Apple releases as open source. These are included in Reef under their own licences:

  • Core Foundation, from swift-corelibs-foundation (Apache 2.0)
  • Grand Central Dispatch, which apps use to run work in the background, from swift-corelibs-libdispatch (Apache 2.0)
  • the Swift standard library and runtime, from swiftlang/swift (Apache 2.0)
  • LZFSE, Apple’s compression format, from lzfse/lzfse (BSD 3-Clause)

We also read objc4, dyld, xnu and Libc from apple-oss-distributions to understand how the Mac behaves, without copying from them. Reef’s Objective-C runtime and loader are our own. Reef also includes LLVM’s libc++, libc++abi and libunwind, SQLite, curl and Tcl. Thanks to everyone behind these projects.

Darling and Wine

Darling is the best-known project for running macOS software on Linux, and Wine has done the same for Windows apps for decades. Wine isn’t an emulator. It reimplements the Windows programming interfaces, and Reef takes the same approach for the Mac, so “Wine for Mac apps” is a reasonable way to think about it.

The difference is mostly scope. Darling aims to run macOS software in general. It is well ahead of us on command-line tools and the system layer underneath, and it works on any Linux desktop. Wine runs a huge range of Windows software across Linux desktops. Reef only targets graphical Mac apps, only on Cutefish, and is built around Cutefish’s own toolkit, compositor and shell. Command-line tools aren’t something we’re aiming for.

We have a lot of respect for what both communities have built.

Is it open source?

Not for now. This is a large investment and a feature that sets Cutefish apart, and it needs to be protected while it grows. Opening it later is possible, for example once community sponsorship can sustain the work.

What’s next

More apps and more of SwiftUI, so that modern Mac apps work, and after that a web engine, which many apps depend on. We’ll write again when there’s more to show.

item.title: Letting agents use the desktop
item.description: How to let Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex or another agent see the Cutefish desktop and use its pointer and keyboard, with your permission.
item.content:encoded:
Agents like Claude Code and Codex can already read files and run commands. With cutefish-computer-use they can also see the screen, click, type and move windows, so they can work with graphical applications the way you do. It is an MCP server: any agent app that supports MCP can use it.

Control goes through cutefish-compositor itself, not a screen recorder and a fake keyboard. The compositor decides when an agent may act, shows that it is acting, and stops it the moment you want.

What keeps you in charge

  • You say yes first. The first time an agent tries to use the desktop, Cutefish asks you. The agent cannot click, type into or fake this dialog. It asks again next time, unless you choose to always allow that app; Settings › Privacy lists those apps and takes them off again.
  • You can always see it, and stop it. While an agent is in control, a Stop button sits in the status bar. Locking the screen stops it too.
  • Your input wins. Moving the pointer or typing pauses the agent until you are done.
  • It cannot answer for you. Permission prompts, password dialogs and the lock screen are off limits to it.
  • Only one program is trusted. The compositor offers control only to /usr/bin/cutefish-computer-use, and the screen can only be read while you have allowed control.

Install

cutefish-computer-use comes with Cutefish Desktop. If your system does not have it yet, install it from the Cutefish repository:

sudo apt install cutefish-computer-use

Then log out and back in: the compositor looks for the server when the session starts.

Claude Code, Codex and other command-line agents

Add it as a stdio MCP server. For Claude Code:

claude mcp add cutefish -- /usr/bin/cutefish-computer-use

For Codex, add this to ~/.codex/config.toml:

[mcp_servers.cutefish]
command = "/usr/bin/cutefish-computer-use"

Other agents take the same command in their MCP settings.

Claude Desktop

Open Settings, then Developer, and choose Edit config. Add the server to claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "cutefish": {
      "command": "/usr/bin/cutefish-computer-use"
    }
  }
}

Restart Claude Desktop. The Developer page now lists cutefish as running.

Trying it

Ask for something that needs the screen, such as “Take a screenshot of my desktop and tell me which apps are in the Dock.” Claude Desktop first asks whether it may use the tool:

Claude Desktop asks this once for each tool. Choose Always allow so it does not ask again; the dialog that decides whether an agent may use your desktop is the next one, and it comes from Cutefish. In Claude Code, allow mcp__cutefish with /permissions for the same effect.

Cutefish then asks whether the agent may control the computer. This dialog comes from the compositor, not from the agent, and the agent cannot answer it. Tick Always allow this app if you do not want to be asked again:

Once you allow it, the agent sees the desktop and gets to work. The Stop button in the status bar shows that it is in control; press it whenever you want it to stop.

What it can do

  • See: screenshots of the desktop or of one window, and zoomed views of part of the screen.
  • Point: click, double-click, drag, scroll and hold buttons.
  • Type: text in any language, key chords and the session’s own shortcuts.
  • Windows and apps: list, focus, move, resize and close windows, open applications, files and links, and set the clipboard.

Bug reports and ideas are welcome on GitHub.

item.title: How Cutefish packages are built, and how to check them
item.description: Cutefish packages and ISOs are built in the open by a public workflow, signed only by that workflow, and every file can be traced back to the build that made it.
item.content:encoded:
Cutefish Desktop now has an APT repository for Debian 13 at download.cutefish.org, and nightly ISOs for testing. Installing a package means trusting whoever built it, so we built the pipeline to need as little trust as possible, and to let you check every step yourself instead of taking our word for it.

In short

  • No one builds by hand. Every package and ISO is built by a public GitHub Actions workflow, from public source, on a fresh machine that is thrown away afterwards. No developer’s computer is involved.
  • No one signs by hand. The key that signs the repository is a secret only that workflow can use. Apart from an offline backup, it is never on anyone’s computer.
  • Every file can be traced. Each one has a public, signed record of the exact repository, commit and build that produced it, kept in a transparency log that nobody, including us, can rewrite.
  • Tampering is caught. APT refuses a changed or swapped file, because it no longer matches the signed index, and the file fails the provenance check too.

Built in the open

No package in the repository is built on a developer’s computer or on a server we run. Every package is built by GitHub Actions on GitHub-hosted machines, in a fresh Debian 13 container that is thrown away after each build.

Everything that goes into a build is public:

  • The source code comes straight from the project repositories under github.com/cutefishos.
  • The packaging and the build steps are in the packaging repository. The workflow that builds and publishes the packages is .github/workflows/build.yml, and anyone can read what it does.
  • Build tools and libraries come from the official Debian archive.
  • Skia, the graphics library the toolkit uses, is fetched at a fixed revision from Google’s own repository, skia.googlesource.com.

The log of every build is public, too. You can open any run on the Actions page and read every command it ran and everything it printed.

Every package names its commit

Nightly packages carry the commit they were built from in their version. For example, 0.1.0+git20261019175928.ef1a42b-1 was built from commit ef1a42b, made on October 19, 2026 at 17:59:28 UTC. To see the exact code inside a package, look up that commit in the project’s repository.

The repository serves the source packages next to the binary ones, so you can also download the source of any package with apt source and compare it with GitHub.

Each build also lists exactly what it used and what it made, at the end of its log and on the run’s summary page:

  • commits: the commit of the packaging repository and of every project that went into the build.
  • SHA256SUMS: the SHA-256 checksum of every file the build produced.

Both are published with the packages, at https://download.cutefish.org/debian/dists/trixie-nightly/commits and https://download.cutefish.org/debian/dists/trixie-nightly/SHA256SUMS.

Tracing a file back to its build

For every file it produces, the build also creates a signed build provenance attestation. It records which repository, which workflow, which commit and which run produced the file with a given checksum. GitHub signs it through Sigstore, not with any key of ours, and it is recorded in Sigstore’s public transparency log, so it cannot be quietly created or changed afterwards.

To check a package you downloaded, use the GitHub CLI, version 2.49 or later, signed in with gh auth login. The gh package in Debian 13 is older; get a current one from cli.github.com.

apt download cutefish-core
gh attestation verify cutefish-core_*.deb --repo cutefishos/packaging

If the file was not built by the Cutefish workflow, or was changed in any way after it was built, the check fails. If it passes, the output links to the exact workflow run, whose full log you can read.

The ISO

The live ISO is built the same way, by .github/workflows/iso.yml in the same repository, from the live-build configuration next to it. It installs the Cutefish packages from download.cutefish.org and everything else from the official Debian archive. Nightly ISOs are published on download.cutefish.org, each with three files:

  • .iso: the image.
  • .iso.sha256: its SHA-256 checksum.
  • .packages: every package in the image, with its version.

LATEST-amd64 and LATEST-arm64 name the newest one for each architecture. To download it, check its checksum and verify its attestation:

name=$(curl -fsSL https://download.cutefish.org/iso/nightly/LATEST-amd64)
curl -fLO "https://download.cutefish.org/iso/nightly/$name.iso"
curl -fLO "https://download.cutefish.org/iso/nightly/$name.iso.sha256"
curl -fLO "https://download.cutefish.org/iso/nightly/$name.packages"
sha256sum -c "$name.iso.sha256"
gh attestation verify "$name.iso" --repo cutefishos/packaging

Every Cutefish package in .packages carries its commit in its version, as above, so you can trace the whole image back to its source.

Signed by the build, and only the build

APT checks the signature of the repository before it installs anything from it. The Cutefish repository is signed with this key:

Cutefish Archive <reionwong@gmail.com>
ed25519, fingerprint 5F52 7F0C B976 4BA0 AF99  BAE5 F4A4 30BC 9E10 91A7

The private key is stored as an encrypted secret of the packaging repository. Only the build workflow can read it, and nothing else ever signs with it. Apart from that secret, the only copy is an offline backup. Releases are not signed by hand on someone’s laptop.

Uploading to download.cutefish.org works the same way: the storage behind it only accepts uploads with a key that, again, only the build workflow holds.

Installing

Download the key, check that its fingerprint matches the one above, and add the repository:

sudo curl -fsSLo /etc/apt/keyrings/cutefish.asc https://download.cutefish.org/debian/cutefish.asc
gpg --show-keys /etc/apt/keyrings/cutefish.asc
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/cutefish.asc] https://download.cutefish.org/debian trixie-nightly main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/cutefish.list
sudo apt update
sudo apt install cutefish-desktop

signed-by limits the key to this repository, so it cannot vouch for packages from anywhere else.

What an attacker would need

Suppose someone wants to get a malicious package onto your computer through Cutefish:

  • Replacing a file on download.cutefish.org is not enough. APT checks every package against the signed index, and the index against the signing key, so a swapped file is refused. Its provenance check fails as well.
  • Stealing the signing key is not enough either: the key alone cannot upload anything to download.cutefish.org. Even with the upload key as well, a package built anywhere else has no attestation from the Cutefish workflow, so it fails the provenance check. Only a run of that workflow, with its public log, can produce one.
  • Changing the source means pushing a commit to a public repository. It shows up in the history, and the build that picks it up names that commit in the package version and in commits.
  • Changing the build means changing the workflow, which is public and versioned in the same way, and every run’s log shows what it did.

Pull requests and forks never see the signing key or the upload key; GitHub only gives secrets to workflows running in the repository itself. The upload key can write to the Cutefish storage bucket and nothing else.

What remains is GitHub’s own infrastructure, which builds the packages, and Sigstore, which records the attestations. We rely on them, as most open source projects do.

What this does not cover

The packages are not yet reproducible: building the same commit twice does not produce byte-identical files, so you cannot rebuild a package yourself and compare checksums. That is something we would like to get to.

trixie-nightly is built from the latest code every night. It is meant for testing, and things in it can break.

Only from official sources

Packages and ISOs from anywhere other than download.cutefish.org and github.com/cutefishos were not built by us.
